positions.stakeholder_concern: In screening settings, under-referral risks missing serious disease in populations with little other healthcare contact, while over-referral imposes real time and travel costs on patients and, if repeated, can erode trust and discourage future screening engagement.
positions.requested_fda_action: Account for both directions of escalation error, and in weighing over-escalation include downstream patient burdens such as travel time and cost and loss of trust that reduces future participation in screening.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The commenter identifies harms from over-referral that are not clinical misdiagnosis but operational and behavioral—patient time and travel costs and erosion of trust leading to disengagement from screening.

positions.public_summary: Drawing on screening experience with borderline readings, the commenter agrees both error directions matter but urges FDA to weigh over-escalation harms beyond clinical risk, including patients' travel time and cost and repeated false referrals eroding trust and future screening participation.
positions.source_passage: In our screenings, this trade-off shows up with borderline readings. Under-referring risks missing something serious in a population that often has no other contact with the healthcare system. But over-referring for every borderline case has real costs for our patients too. It's a real cost for these people to take the time and spend the money traveling to clinics, and it can also make them distrust future screenings if it happens repeatedly, which discourages them from engaging with the healthcare system at all.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter believes the acceptable balance between under- and over-escalation is context-dependent, varying with how difficult the escalation resource is to access, the population-level benefit, and existing population trust in the system, so a uniform error rate would not fit settings with very different resource constraints.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should require manufacturers to justify how escalation thresholds are calibrated to the specific population and care access context in which the device is deployed, instead of applying a single acceptable error rate across all settings.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment ties acceptable escalation performance to the specific deployment setting's resource constraints and population, implying assurance must be established per-context rather than once globally.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: It frames over-escalation error tolerance in terms of resource availability and access difficulty, i.e., strain on constrained care capacity rather than only direct clinical harm.

positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's attention to under- and over-escalation errors, but argues the acceptable balance is context-dependent, shaped by resource access, population benefit, and trust. Asks CDRH to require manufacturers to justify escalation threshold calibration for each deployment population and care-access setting, not a single error rate.
positions.source_passage: I think the right balance depends heavily on context, including how difficult it is to access the resource, how much benefit it would bring the population, and how much trust the population already has in the system. I'd encourage CDRH to require that manufacturers justify their calibration of escalation thresholds against the specific population and care access context the device is deployed in, rather than applying a single acceptable error rate across settings with very different resource constraints.
